title: Six directions
hook: young Sigala bows to the six directions; the Buddha gives the bow a meaning
carry: each direction has a face in it

segments.voice: Yesterday: four kings and a verse for the forest. Your line: protection. Today a discourse begins that this path will walk for six days, and it opens with a young man soaking wet.

Early morning, outside Rajagaha. A young householder named Sigala has bathed, and still in wet clothes, with wet hair, he raises his joined hands and bows. To the east. The south. The west. The north. Below. Above. Six directions, one after another. The Buddha, walking into town for alms, stops and asks what he's doing. Sigala answers simply: my father, as he was dying, told me to honor the directions. So I do, out of respect for his words.
screen: `WET HAIR, JOINED HANDS.` → `EAST, SOUTH, WEST, NORTH, BELOW, ABOVE.` → `MY FATHER ASKED ME TO.`

segments.voice: Here's what the Buddha doesn't do. He doesn't tell Sigala to stop, or call the custom empty, or his father wrong. He says: that isn't quite how the six directions are honored in the noble discipline. Curious, Sigala asks: then how? Please teach me. So the Buddha keeps the bow and gives it a meaning. This is the Sigalovada, the advice to Sigala, the thirty-first Long Discourse, which an old commentary calls the householder's discipline. First he clears the ground. A wise person avoids four ways of acting that stain a life: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct and lying. He avoids four motives for doing wrong, which open tomorrow, and six ways wealth leaks away, the day after. Only then does he return to the bow. The six directions are six relationships. East, the direction of the sunrise, is your parents, who came first. South is your teachers. West is your partner and children. North is your friends. Below are those who work for you. Above are the spiritual teachers in your life. Honor each of them, he says, and each will care for you in return. A grieving son's ritual, done for love of his father, isn't thrown away. It's filled. The same bow, the same six turns. Only now each direction has a face in it.
screen: `HE DOESN'T TELL HIM TO STOP.` · `FIRST, CLEAR THE GROUND.` · `SIX DIRECTIONS, SIX RELATIONSHIPS.` · `THE SAME BOW, WITH FACES IN IT.` · then, large: `SIX DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: If you're able, face east, the morning sun's side, and with joined hands or a simple nod honor your parents, or whoever raised you. Turn right to the south for your teachers, behind you to the west for your partner, children and household, left to the north for your friends, then down for people who work with or for you, and up for anyone who has guided you in what matters most. A face for each, then sit.
Six directions. In DN 31 Sigala bows to them for his father's sake, and the Buddha makes them six relationships: parents, teachers, family, friends, workers, guides. Today's word.
Your line: each direction has a face in it. The bow stays; its meaning grows. That's day five hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers teach the Sigalovada Sutta to lay people as a guide to family and social life, and some use the six directions as a way to remember the relationships it describes.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. a young man is bowing to the six directions because his dying father asked him to. what do you say?
options: that the custom is empty and he should stop.
that this isn't quite how the noble discipline honors the directions, and when he asks, teach him.
fork.reveal: he keeps Sigala's practice and fills it with meaning: six directions become six relationships.

original.note: Pali disa: direction, quarter. Sigala bows to the six disa.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha dismissed old rituals.
what it means: here he keeps the ritual and gives it new content: each direction is a relationship.
what a scholar hears: DN 31 reinterprets a ritual (disa-namassana) in the 'noble discipline' (ariyassa vinaye), a pattern seen elsewhere in the canon with brahmanical practices.

chat.says: Why didn't the Buddha just tell that young man to stop bowing to the sky?
options: He kept the bow and filled it: each direction became a relationship to honor.
He did; he said bowing is useless and told him to meditate instead.
He thought the father's custom was wrong, but too old to argue with.
chat.meaning: In DN 31 the Buddha doesn't stop Sigala's bow; he gives it meaning: parents, teachers, family, friends, workers and spiritual teachers.
